title: Speech Privacy in Buildings

findings.antecedent: Average Transmission Loss (TL) rating of isolating wall
findings.consequent: Observed reaction to privacy (Extreme Dissatisfaction to Apparent Satisfaction)
findings.mechanism: The categorization scheme based on average TL is inadequate because other acoustical factors are important for speech privacy.
findings.quote: But it is clear from Fig. 1 that an average transmission loss of 35 db is not the demarcation between satisfaction and dissatisfaction.

findings.antecedent: Increase in background noise level
findings.mechanism: Speech peaks are submerged by steady background noise (masking effect).
findings.quote: The intelligibility of intruding speech is destroyed when the speech peaks are submerged in steady background noise

findings.antecedent: Increase in transmission loss (TL)
findings.mechanism: Reduction of the speech signal relative to noise, similar to increasing background noise.
findings.quote: an increase in the background level has the same effect on intelligibility as an increase in the transmission loss.

findings.antecedent: Different buildings/locations
findings.consequent: Background noise levels in speech-frequency bands
findings.mechanism: Varying sources of background noise (e.g., traffic, air-conditioning terminal devices).
findings.quote: Figure 2 shows that background levels in the speech-frequency bands vary from building to building by 30 db or more.

findings.antecedent: Published (laboratory) vs. field measurements of Transmission Loss (TL)
findings.mechanism: Incomplete test samples, panel size and boundary damping, special test conditions, and obsolete data in published values.
findings.quote: it is not uncommon to find differences in the order of 10 db or more between the advertised transmission-loss values of a partition, and the data obtained from a valid field measurement

findings.antecedent: Room size (small 6x8 ft office vs. large 40x40 ft classroom)
findings.consequent: Reverberant speech levels (for constant speech power)
findings.mechanism: Sound-absorbing area (Sā) is approximately equal to the floor area, which varies with room size.
findings.quote: Assuming a constant speech power, the corresponding range in reverberant speech levels is 15 db.

findings.antecedent: Ratio of wall area to listener-room floor area (1:2 to 2:1)
findings.mechanism: Geometric factors affecting sound transmission.
findings.quote: Figure 4 shows a range of ratios of wall area to listener-room floor area from 1 to 2; the corresponding variation in transmitted levels is 6 db.

findings.antecedent: Speech effort (conversational vs. raised vs. loud voice)
findings.mechanism: Increased vocal effort directly increases sound power level.
findings.quote: The sound levels for a 'raised voice' are about 6 db higher than those for conversational speech; a 'loud voice' is about 12 db higher.

findings.antecedent: Privacy requirement (normal vs. confidential work)
findings.consequent: Tolerated intelligibility of intruding speech (or required speech signal to background noise ratio)
findings.mechanism: Different cognitive demands and social implications of privacy levels lead to different tolerance thresholds for intelligibility.
findings.quote: Generally, this amounted to a 6-db difference in the ratio of speech signal to background noise.

findings.antecedent: Varying background noise levels (within NC-20 to NC-35 range)
findings.mechanism: Privacy judgment is based on the relative signal-to-noise ratio, not the absolute level of background noise.
findings.quote: The data of Fig. 9 show that on the average our test subjects responded with a constant signal-to-noise ratio as the background levels varied.

findings.antecedent: Repeated judgments by subjects
findings.mechanism: Subjects generally give consistent responses after a short learning period.
findings.quote: during one day of testing, 13 subjects made 356 judgments of privacy. The rms variation from their average responses was 1.3 db.

findings.antecedent: Subject criticality (least vs. most critical)
findings.mechanism: Individual differences in perception and tolerance for intruding speech.
findings.quote: When asked to define 'normal' or everyday privacy, the least critical subject allowed 20-db higher speech levels than the most critical.

findings.antecedent: Subject criticality (range)
findings.mechanism: Individual differences in perception and tolerance for intruding speech, even for confidential tasks.
findings.quote: When defining 'confidential' privacy, the maximum variation among subjects was about 10 db.

findings.antecedent: Privacy requirement (normal vs. confidential) for most critical subjects
findings.mechanism: The perceived importance of privacy for confidential tasks leads to a lower tolerance for intruding speech.
findings.quote: There was a shift of about 6 db between the definitions of 'normal' and 'confidential' privacy as given by the most critical subjects.

findings.antecedent: Wall type ('flat' wall with weak low-frequency speech components vs. other walls)
findings.mechanism: The spectral characteristics of the intruding speech (e.g., weak low-frequency components) influence its perceived intelligibility and annoyance, even at a given AI.
findings.quote: It appears that both the most critical 10% of the subjects and the average subject tolerated a higher articulation index for the 'flat' wall

findings.antecedent: Unintelligible, narrow-band speech (especially low frequencies)
findings.mechanism: Even if speech is unintelligible, its presence, especially in certain frequency bands, can still be perceived as annoying.
findings.quote: Thus, we do find annoyance caused by unintelligible, narrow-band speech, especially at the low frequencies.

findings.antecedent: Bandwidth of intruding speech (1/3-octave 250 cps vs. wider bands)
findings.mechanism: Narrower bands contribute less to overall speech intelligibility.
findings.quote: The AI for the 250 cps, 1/3-octave was only 2% when the subject responded. This compares with 5-10% for the wider bandwidths.

findings.antecedent: 10-dB dip in TL (one 1/3-octave band wide)
findings.mechanism: The effect of a narrow TL dip is small and accounted for by the articulation-index rating scheme.
findings.quote: As may be seen, a 10-db dip only one-third octave wide was judged to be relatively unimportant.

findings.antecedent: 15-dB dip in TL at lower frequencies
findings.mechanism: Low-frequency narrow bands of speech have a larger function relating annoyance to signal-to-noise ratio than to intelligibility.
findings.quote: As may be seen, there is a response which at the lower frequencies is not predicted by the change in the articulation index caused by the dip.

findings.antecedent: Ratio of intruding speech to ambient noise vs. level of speech itself
findings.mechanism: Privacy perception is driven by the masking effect of background noise on intruding speech, not the absolute loudness of the speech.
findings.quote: The typical test subject's feeling of privacy appears to be related to the ratio of the intruding speech to the ambient or background noise rather than to the level of the speech itself.

findings.antecedent: Articulation Index (AI)
findings.mechanism: AI quantifies speech intelligibility, which is a primary determinant of perceived speech privacy.
findings.quote: More particularly, the subject reaction seems to be correlated with the articulation index which is a 'weighted' signal-to-noise ratio.

findings.antecedent: Articulation Index (AI) reaching 0.05
findings.mechanism: AI of 0.05 represents a threshold of intelligibility beyond which privacy is compromised for critical subjects.
findings.quote: the most critical 10% of the subjects began to feel a lack of privacy when the articulation index reached 0.05.

findings.antecedent: Total rating computed from proposed scheme (integrating source room size, speech use, background noise, noise reduction, privacy requirement)
findings.mechanism: The scheme integrates multiple acoustical and social factors that collectively determine speech intelligibility and privacy perception in real-world settings.
findings.quote: The most significant fact about Fig. 20 is the fairly tight grouping of the data.

findings.antecedent: Articulation Index (AI) of 0.05
findings.mechanism: AI of 0.05 represents a critical threshold for perceived privacy, marking the transition from satisfaction to dissatisfaction.
findings.quote: situations with an articulation index of 0.05 are more or less on the borderline between apparent satisfaction and some degree of dissatisfaction.

findings.antecedent: Small change in noise reduction or background noise
findings.consequent: Significant variation in occupant's reaction to privacy
findings.mechanism: The relationship between physical acoustic parameters and subjective privacy perception is steep near the privacy threshold, indicating high sensitivity to small changes.
findings.quote: the slope of the curve in Fig. 20 is quite steep. This means that a small change in the noise reduction or background noise can make a significant variation in the occupant's reaction.

findings.antecedent: Increase in signal-to-noise ratio by 10 dB
findings.mechanism: A direct relationship exists between the signal-to-noise ratio and the ability to understand speech.
findings.quote: on the average, an increase in the signal-to-noise ratio of only 10 or so db would be expected to result in fairly complete sentence intelligibility.

findings.antecedent: Occasional loud talker / self talking loudly
findings.mechanism: Social norms and personal control over sound production influence privacy expectations and allowances.
findings.quote: most occupants desire privacy on the average but may be willing to make allowances for the occasional loud talker and do not expect privacy when they themselves talk loudly.

stimuli.description: Simulated private-office environments with adjacent rooms, physical walls, spectrum-shaping filters, and attenuators. Intruding speech was a shorthand-training recording played via loudspeaker. Background noise was a 2-channel tape recording of traffic and diffuser noise.
Real-life building environments (offices, hospitals, dormitories, motels) for case history analysis.

tables.description: Example of commonly used 'categorization scheme' showing recommended average transmission loss (db) for different types of spaces (e.g., private offices, hotels, classrooms).
Recommended acceptable average noise levels ('A' scale levels db) in unoccupied rooms for various categories of space (e.g., hospitals, conference rooms, restaurants).
Characteristic noise levels (db) for N, L, M, and H noise spectra at 30 dB across octave and 1/3-octave bands.
Weighting factors for rating noise curves across five octave bands (150-300 cps to 2400-4800 cps).
Sound-power level (db re 10^-13 w) and importance function (multiplied by 6000) of normal speech for 1/3-octave and 1-octave bands.

Summary of 37 case-history data, including descriptions of space and construction, rating factors (source room size, speech use, background noise, noise reduction, privacy requirement), total computed rating, and observed subjective reaction to privacy.

limitations: Studies were strictly limited to speech as the intruding signal.
Laboratory studies were performed in the context of a typical office situation.
Field study and case histories were mostly office situations, with limited data from hospitals, dormitories, and motels.
Applicability to other kinds of spaces (e.g., apartments) needs further verification.
Studies were restricted to buildings in the United States, and the average response curve may shift laterally in other countries.
The probable total uncertainty in estimating the five items of the proposed rating scheme is ±4 or 5 dB, requiring an accuracy of ±2 dB for each component for overall accuracy.
